summary: Defines S/MIME version 3.2, a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. It provides digital signatures for authentication and integrity and encryption for confidentiality. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 8551.

eli5.summary: S/MIME lets you sign an email so people know it is from you, and seal it so only the right person can read it. This version describes the details. It was replaced by RFC 8551.

questions: how to sign and encrypt email with s/mime
subtitle: How to sign, encrypt and compress MIME messages so email and other MIME traffic can be secured end to end.

tldr.problem: Internet messages built on MIME had no consistent way to carry digital signatures or encryption that any compliant mail program could create and read.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME 3.2 wraps a prepared MIME entity in a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) object and carries it in application/pkcs7-mime, or uses multipart/signed with a detached application/pkcs7-signature. It also fixes which algorithms and attributes agents must support.
tldr.outcome: Messages can be signed, encrypted, compressed, or a nested combination. This RFC obsoletes RFC 3851 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 8551.

today: RFC 5751 is obsoleted by RFC 8551, which is the newer S/MIME message specification. It replaced RFC 3851 when published in January 2010.

sections.title: What S/MIME Provides
sections.content:
S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) gives a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Digital signatures provide authentication, message integrity and non-repudiation of origin. Encryption provides data confidentiality. Compression is a supplementary service that reduces size.

It is not limited to mail. It can be used with any transport that carries MIME data, such as HTTP or SIP, and by automated agents, for example to sign software-generated documents. The specification separates requirements for sending agents and receiving agents, and generally follows the rule of being liberal in what you receive and conservative in what you send.

It defines how to build a MIME body part protected under the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) of RFC 5652, which derives from PKCS #7. Agents must also follow the CMS algorithm and SHA-2 documents it references.
sections.eli5: S/MIME is a set of rules for putting a signature and a lock on a message. It works for email and for other things that carry messages.

sections.title: Required Algorithms and Attributes
sections.content:
Section 2 sets a baseline so all implementations can talk to each other. Besides the usual MUST and SHOULD, the RFC adds SHOULD+ (expected to become a MUST later), SHOULD- (expected to become a MAY) and MUST- (a MUST that may relax in a future document).

  • Digests: agents MUST support SHA-256 and SHOULD- support SHA-1.
  • Signatures: MUST support RSA with SHA-256. DSA with SHA-256 and RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256 are SHOULD+.
  • Key encryption: MUST support RSA encryption; RSAES-OAEP is SHOULD+; Diffie-Hellman ephemeral-static is SHOULD-.
  • Content encryption: MUST support AES-128 CBC; AES-192 CBC and AES-256 CBC are SHOULD+; tripleDES is SHOULD-.

Sending agents SHOULD include signed attributes such as Signing Time, SMIMECapabilities and Encryption Key Preference. SMIMECapabilities lists, in order of preference, what the signer can decrypt, and receiving agents remember it to choose algorithms for replies. Receivers must handle unknown values gracefully.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to agree on a few basic locks and pens so any two mail programs can understand each other. A signature can also say which kinds of locks its owner likes best.

sections.title: Building S/MIME Messages
sections.content:
The data to be secured is always a canonical MIME entity. It is prepared in three steps: apply local conventions, convert leaf parts to canonical form (text must use CR LF line endings), then apply transfer encoding. The CMS object produced is then wrapped in MIME.

The application/pkcs7-mime media type carries SignedData, EnvelopedData and CompressedData. Senders SHOULD add an smime-type parameter as a hint:

  • enveloped-data for EnvelopedData
  • signed-data for SignedData
  • certs-only for a certificate management message
  • compressed-data for CompressedData

For signing there are two formats. In application/pkcs7-mime with SignedData the content is inside the signature, so recipients without S/MIME cannot view it, but benign intermediaries cannot break it. In multipart/signed, a clear-signing format, the first part is the signed entity and the second is a detached application/pkcs7-signature, so anyone can read it. The multipart/signed form is generally preferred for sending, and receivers MUST handle both. Its protocol parameter MUST be application/pkcs7-signature, and a micalg parameter names the digest, such as sha-256.

Formats can be nested in any order. Signing first hides the signers inside the envelope; encrypting first leaves them visible. Enveloped-only messages give no integrity, since ciphertext could be altered without detection. Files commonly use the extensions .p7m, .p7s, .p7c and .p7z.
sections.eli5: You first tidy the message into a standard shape, then either seal it inside the signature envelope or attach the signature beside it so anyone can still read the letter.

sections.title: Certificates and Key Sizes
sections.content:
This RFC does not say how certificates are validated; that is left to the companion certificate-handling document, RFC 5750. It only says what happens once a certificate is validated or rejected. Agents MUST provide some way to retrieve recipients' certificates, and SHOULD let users store and protect those of correspondents.

Key pairs MUST come from a good source of non-deterministic random input, and the private key MUST be protected. An agent MUST NOT generate asymmetric keys under 512 bits for RSA or DSA signatures. For keys of 1024 to 2048 bits, generating signatures and encrypting SHOULD be done and verifying and decrypting MUST be supported. Keys of 1023 bits or fewer SHOULD NOT be used to sign or encrypt, though receivers MAY accept them. Larger keys are a MAY.
sections.eli5: Your secret key has to be hard to guess, and short keys are too easy to crack. Other people's keys must be findable so you can lock messages for them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that cryptographic algorithms are broken or weakened over time, so implementers should keep checking. It chose a 2048-bit RSA key size to provide at least 100 bits of security. Weak cryptography offers little actual security over plaintext and is never recommended unless the only alternative is no cryptography.

RSA and DSA keys of less than 1024 bits are considered by many experts to be insecure. An implementation that verifies signatures made with such keys MUST warn the user, while servers where warnings are not appropriate SHOULD reject them. Attackers could also send certificates with very large keys to cause excessive processing, so agents should manage cryptographic resources.

Other cautions: a sender SHOULD NOT send a copy of a message with weaker cryptography than the original, because an attacker could decrypt the weak copy; encrypted data without authentication can be modified undetected; and software that changes its behavior because a message appears signed should first verify the signature.
sections.eli5: Locks get weaker as burglars get smarter, so use strong ones. Do not send the same letter in a flimsy box as well as a strong one, or the thief will just open the flimsy one.
